title: The Data Science Workflow End-to-End
summary: Having learned many individual skills, this day steps back to connect them into the single coherent workflow that professional data scientists follow, so the capstone doesn't feel like a jumble of techniques. Revisiting the CRISP-DM framework (Busine
content:
# The Data Science Workflow End-to-End ##### "Build us a churn model" A data scientist joined a subscription business in Pune and received exactly that brief. She spent six weeks building an excellent model — 0.86 AUC, well-calibrated, properly validated, deployed behind an API. Nobody used it. The retention team had no budget for interventions and no process for acting on a risk score. The customer success team had eleven people and 40,000 at-risk customers. And the actual business problem, which nobody had articulated, was not "which customers will churn" — it was "which of the 200 customers we have capacity to call this month should we call." That is a different question. It needs a ranked list with expected recoverable value, not a probability for everyone. Two weeks of work, and it would have shipped. You now have thirty-nine days of individual skills. Today is about the frame that connects them, because the most common cause of failed data science projects is not weak modelling — it is solving the wrong problem well. ##### CRISP-DM, revisited with skills attached You met CRISP-DM on day one as an abstract diagram. Now every stage maps to things you can actually do. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["1. BUSINESS UNDERSTANDING
What decision changes?"] --> B["2. DATA UNDERSTANDING
EDA, quality audit, profiling"] B --> C["3. DATA PREPARATION
Cleaning, features, pipelines"] C --> D["4. MODELING
Baseline, candidates, tuning"] D --> E["5. EVALUATION
Metrics, error analysis, business value"] E --> F["6. DEPLOYMENT
Streamlit, report, monitoring"] E -->|Does not meet the goal| A B -->|Data cannot answer this| A C -->|Quality too poor| B F --> G[Monitor and iterate] --> A ``` | Stage | Your tools | Typical time | |---|---|---| | Business understanding | Stakeholder conversations, problem framing | 5–10% | | Data understanding | Pandas, EDA, profiling, SQL | **25–30%** | | Data preparation | Cleaning, feature engineering, pipelines | **30–40%** | | Modeling | scikit-learn, boosting, cross-validation | 10–15% | | Evaluation | Metrics, error analysis, fairness audit | 10% | | Deployment | Streamlit, joblib, reporting | 10% | Two things in that table surprise beginners. **Modelling is the smallest technical stage** — often a single afternoon. And **the loop back from Evaluation to Business Understanding is the most-travelled arrow**, because the first framing is usually wrong in some way you can only discover by trying. ##### From business question to data question This translation is the highest-leverage skill in the whole workflow, and it is almost never taught. A business question is vague, contextual and about outcomes. A data question is precise, measurable and about a specific prediction or comparison. | Business question | Data question | |---|---| | "Why are we losing customers?" | "Which observable behaviours in the first 60 days predict cancellation within 90 days, and how much of the variation do they explain?" | | "Should we open a store in Nashik?" | "Given demographics, competitor density and footfall for our existing 47 stores, what is the predicted first-year revenue for a Nashik location, with a prediction interval?" | | "Is our marketing working?" | "Did the campaign cohort show higher 30-day retention than a matched control, and by how much with what confidence?" | | "Make our support better" | "Can we route incoming tickets to the correct team with ≥85% precision per team, reducing median resolution time?" | The translation questions to ask, in order: **1. What decision will change based on this?** If the answer is "we'll know more", stop. That is not a project. **2. Who makes that decision, how often, and what are their constraints?** The Pune case failed here — the constraint was eleven people and 200 calls a month, and nobody asked. **3. What does "better" mean numerically?** Convert the goal into a metric with a target. "Reduce churn" becomes "reduce 90-day churn in the 3–6 month cohort from 34% to under 28%". **4. What would you do today without a model?** This is your baseline and often 80% of the value. If the honest answer is "call the customers who have not logged in for 30 days", your model must beat that rule. **5. What data exists, and is it available at prediction time?** A feature populated after the outcome is leakage, and this question catches it early. ##### Choosing methods by stage Beginners over-apply techniques because they have just learned them. A quick reference for choosing deliberately: **Data understanding.** Always: `shape`, `head`, `info`, `describe`, `isna().sum()`, distributions per column, target relationships, correlation matrix. Add `ydata-profiling` for wide data. Add domain conversations for anything you cannot interpret. **Data preparation.** Missing values — understand *why* before choosing a strategy, and add a missingness indicator. Categoricals — one-hot below ~15 levels, frequency encoding above. Scaling — required for k-NN, SVM, neural networks and regularised linear models; irrelevant for trees. Always inside a `Pipeline`. **Modeling.** Structure the escalation: ``` 1. Dummy baseline (what does no skill look like?) 2. Business-rule baseline (what does the current process achieve?) 3. Linear/logistic (interpretable, fast, often close) 4. Random Forest (strong, forgiving, no tuning) 5. Gradient boosting (usually the best on tabular data) 6. Neural network (only if 1-5 are insufficient AND you have the data) ``` Stop as soon as you have something that clears the bar. A logistic regression that meets the target and ships this month beats a boosted ensemble that meets it 1.5% better next quarter. **Evaluation.** Match the metric to the decision: | Situation | Metric | |---|---| | Imbalanced classification | PR-AUC, recall at fixed alert capacity | | Ranking a limited review queue | Precision@k | | Regression with symmetric costs | MAE | | Regression where big errors hurt | RMSE | | Any high-stakes decision | Expected cost in ₹ | The Pune model should have been evaluated on **precision@200** — of the 200 customers flagged for calling, how many would actually have churned — not on AUC across all 40,000. ##### Managing scope Data science projects expand without resistance. Three habits contain that. **Timebox each stage.** Decide in advance: three days for EDA, one week for features, three days for modelling. When the box is spent, move on with what you have. You can always return. **Build the thin slice first.** Get a crude version of the *entire* pipeline working — load, clean minimally, baseline model, evaluate, save — before improving any part of it. An end-to-end pipeline at 60% quality tells you far more than a perfect cleaning step and nothing else. ``` Week 1: crude end-to-end version, working Week 2: improve the stage that most limits performance Week 3: improve the next one ``` That ordering means you always have something to show, and you discover integration problems on day four instead of day thirty. **Write down what you are not doing.** An explicit non-goals list prevents drift and demonstrates judgement: ```markdown ## Non-goals - Not covering B2B accounts (different behaviour, separate project) - Not real-time scoring (a weekly batch meets the business need) - Not building a dashboard (the output is a ranked CSV for the CS team) - Not causal inference (this is prediction; the intervention needs an A/B test) ``` **Know when to stop.** Stop when you meet the success criterion, when the next improvement costs more than it is worth, when the bottleneck is data quality rather than modelling, or when the business need has changed. That last one happens more than people admit. ##### Planning your capstone The next three days build a portfolio project. Choose well, because scope decides whether you finish. Four criteria for a project that will hold up: 1. **Real, messy data you can obtain.** Clean benchmark data lets you skip the work that demonstrates competence. 2. **A plausible business decision behind it**, not just an accuracy number. 3. **One genuinely hard component** — imbalance, a latency constraint, text plus tabular, messy joins. 4. **Explainable in ninety seconds** to someone non-technical. Ideas using data you can actually get in India: | Project | Source | Hard part | |---|---|---| | Consumer complaint routing | Public grievance portals | Multilingual text, class imbalance | | Mandi price forecasting | Agmarknet (data.gov.in) | Time series, missing data, seasonality | | Air quality prediction | CPCB open data | Temporal features, station gaps | | Used vehicle price estimation | Listing sites (check ToS) | Feature engineering, outliers | | Electricity demand forecast | State load despatch data | Strong seasonality, weather joins | | Cricket match outcome | Cricsheet ball-by-ball data | Sequential features, leakage traps | **Scope ruthlessly.** One target, one clearly-stated user, one primary metric. A capstone trying to be a platform becomes an unfinished README. The proposal document to write before starting: ```markdown # Capstone Proposal — Mandi Price Forecasting ## 1. Business problem Farmers and traders in Maharashtra decide when and where to sell produce with limited price visibility. Selling a week early or late can change realised price by 15-30%. ## 2. Decision this supports A farmer choosing between selling this week at the local mandi or waiting. ## 3. Data question Given 5 years of daily arrival and price data for onions across 12 mandis, forecast the modal price 7 days ahead, with a prediction interval. ## 4. Success criteria Primary: MASE < 0.85 against a seasonal-naive baseline on a 6-month temporal holdout. Secondary: 80% prediction intervals achieve 75-85% empirical coverage. Guardrail: forecasts must be produced in under 2 seconds. ## 5. Data Agmarknet daily prices, 2021-2026, ~180,000 rows. Known issues: missing days around holidays, occasional 10x unit errors, mandi name variants. ## 6. Non-goals - Not modelling other crops (onion only in v1) - Not causal analysis of what drives price - Not a mobile app (Streamlit web app is sufficient) ## 7. Planned approach EDA -> temporal features (lags, rolling, seasonality, arrivals) -> seasonal-naive baseline -> LightGBM -> compare -> Streamlit app ## 8. Risks R1: Price series may be near-random at 7-day horizon. Mitigation: test the baseline early; if MASE cannot beat 1.0, reduce horizon to 3 days. R2: Mandi name inconsistency will fragment the data. Mitigation: build and review a mapping table in week 1. ## 9. Timeline Day 41: acquisition + EDA + cleaning Day 42: features + baseline + models + evaluation Day 43: Streamlit app + report + deployment ``` The **Risks** section with concrete mitigations is what makes this read as professional work rather than optimism. R1 in particular is the honest one — testing whether the problem is solvable *before* investing three days is exactly the discipline that separates experienced practitioners from beginners. ##### A checklist for the whole workflow Worth keeping visible while you work: **Framing** — Can I state the decision this changes? Do I have a success criterion with a number? What is the no-model baseline? **Data** — Have I run the five inspection commands? Do I know what every column means? Is every feature available at prediction time? **Preparation** — Is all preprocessing inside a pipeline? Have I checked for leakage? Is the split temporal or grouped if it needs to be? **Modelling** — Did I build a baseline first? Am I comparing on cross-validation, not the test set? Is the test set still untouched? **Evaluation** — Does my metric match the decision? Have I looked at errors by hand? Have I checked performance by subgroup? **Delivery** — Can someone else reproduce this? Is there a README? Does the output reach the person who acts on it? That last question closes the loop back to the Pune failure. A model that does not reach a decision-maker in a form they can act on has produced nothing, however good it is. ##### Common mistakes - Accepting a vague brief without translating it into a data question. - Never asking what the current process is, so you cannot say whether you improved it. - Perfecting one stage before the pipeline runs end to end. - Optimising a metric that does not match the decision. - Building for all customers when capacity constrains you to 200. - Never writing down non-goals, so scope drifts indefinitely. - Escalating to complex models before a baseline is beaten. - Discovering leakage after weeks of work instead of during framing. - Choosing a capstone too large to finish. - Treating deployment as optional. ##### Hands-on Choose your capstone dataset and problem, then write the project plan: business question, data question, success metric with a number, the method you will use at each CRISP-DM stage, and an explicit timebox for each. Before committing, do the feasibility check — load the data, compute the simplest possible baseline, and confirm the problem is tractable. Discovering on day one that a seasonal-naive baseline is already excellent saves three days and is itself a finding worth reporting. For the mini-project, produce a complete capstone proposal using the template above: problem statement, decision supported, data question, success criteria with primary, secondary and guardrail metrics, data source with known quality issues, explicit non-goals, planned approach per stage, risks with concrete mitigations, and a three-day timeline. Have someone else read it and ask them one question — could you tell me, in one sentence, what this project will produce and who will use it? If they cannot, the proposal is not ready. For the assignment, take a vague business question and rewrite it as a precise, measurable data science problem with a clear success criterion. Then add the two questions most people skip: what decision changes as a result, and what would you do today without any model. ##### Key takeaways - Modelling is the smallest technical stage; understanding and preparing data consumes 60–70% of real project time. - Translating a business question into a data question is the highest-leverage skill — always ask what decision changes. - Build the thin end-to-end slice first, then improve the stage that most limits performance. - Escalate models deliberately from a dummy baseline upward, and stop when you clear the bar. - Write down non-goals and risks with mitigations; scope discipline is what turns a plan into a finished project.
